subject: binary
title: Counting With Only 0 and 1
summary: Computers count with just two digits. Each place is worth double the one next to it.

keys.prompt: Why can a computer get by with only 0 and 1?
keys.answer: Its tiny parts are either on or off. On can stand for 1, and off can stand for 0.

options.text: Its parts are on or off, and that can mean 1 or 0
It can only count up to 1
Bigger digits would not fit on the screen

keys.prompt: In binary, what is each place worth compared with the place to its right?
keys.answer: Twice as much. The places go 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, and so on.

keys.prompt: How many different patterns can one byte (8 bits) make?
keys.answer: 256. That is enough for every number from 0 to 255.

cards.title: The flashlight game
cards.text: Say you can only talk to a friend with a flashlight. It can be on or off. That's it! Could you still send your friend the number 9?

cards.question: In binary, you only get the digits 0 and 1. How do you think you write the number 2?
cards.reveal: It's 10! That means one 2 and zero 1s.

cards.title: Just two choices
cards.text: Inside a computer, tiny parts are either on or off. On can mean 1. Off can mean 0. Each 0 or 1 is called a bit. The word bit is short for binary digit.
cards.example: A light switch is like one bit. It is up or down, with nothing in between.

why.q: Why do computers use only two choices, not ten?
why.a: Two choices are simple to build and hard to mix up. Even if a signal is a little messy, on and off still look very different.

cards.title: Places that double
cards.text: In our numbers, each place is worth 10 times more: ones, tens, hundreds. In binary, each place is worth 2 times more: ones, twos, fours, eights. To read a number, add up the places that have a 1.
cards.example: 1001 means one 8 and one 1. So 8 + 1 = 9. And 10 means one 2 and no 1s. So it is 2.

cards.title: Count like a computer
cards.text: Binary counting goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100. When a place is full, it goes back to 0. Then you carry a 1 to the next place on the left. It is the same trick we use to go from 9 to 10.
cards.example: Say your pinky is the 1s place and your ring finger is the 2s place. Finger up is 1. Both up is 11. That is 2 + 1 = 3.

cards.title: Eight bits make a byte
cards.text: A group of 8 bits is called a byte. A byte can make 256 different patterns. That is enough for every number from 0 to 255. Long ago, one byte was often used to store one letter.
cards.example: Each extra bit doubles the patterns. Two bits make 4: 00, 01, 10 and 11. Three bits make 8.

why.q: Why does adding one more bit double the patterns?
why.a: The new bit can be 0 or 1. Each old pattern can go with either one, so you get two times as many.

cards.question: Say you can only flash a light on and off. How could you send a friend a secret word?
nudges: What if each letter got its own number?
How would your friend know where one letter stops?

options.why: Yes. A bit is the smallest piece of computer information.
A group of 8 bits is a byte. A bit is just one 0 or 1.
A bit is not a machine. It is one 0 or 1 inside the machine.
In binary, 11 means one 2 and one 1. Add them up!
Close! 10 is 2. The extra 1 on the right adds one more.

questions.q: How many bits are in a byte?

options.why: Yes. Eight bits make one byte.
Two is how many choices one bit has. A byte has 8 bits.
Ten is how many digits we use. A byte has 8 bits.

sources.title: Binary number
sources.supports: Binary is base 2 and uses only 0 and 1; each digit is a bit; almost all modern computers use it because it is straightforward to implement with logic gates and has noise immunity; in a modern computer bits may be two different voltages, on disks magnetic polarities, earlier switches and punched holes or tape; any mechanism with two exclusive states can represent bits; counting goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100 with reset and carry like decimal; each bit is an increasing power of 2 and the value is the sum, e.g. 100101 = 32 + 4 + 1 = 37; Leibniz's first known binary work was 1679 and his best-known article, Explication de l'Arithmetique Binaire, was published in 1703; he saw 1 and 0 as a symbol of creation out of nothing; Claude Shannon's 1937 MIT master's thesis implemented Boolean algebra and binary arithmetic with relays and switches and essentially founded practical digital circuit design.

sources.title: Bit
sources.supports: The bit is the most basic unit of information in computing; the name is a portmanteau of binary digit; a bit can be stored by a device that exists in either of two states.

sources.title: Byte
sources.supports: A byte commonly consists of eight bits; historically it was the number of bits used to encode one character of text; 2 to the 8th power is 256, so one byte holds the values 0 through 255.
